content.text: From the Moon orbiting Earth to the International Space Station, from GPS satellites to the planets circling the Sun—orbital motion is fundamental to understanding our place in space. This lesson explores how gravity keeps objects in orbit and the different types of satellite orbits used for various purposes.

An orbiting object is in continuous free fall. Gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps it on a curved path. The object moves sideways fast enough that it keeps missing the surface as it falls -- this is what an orbit is.
Object moving in a circle needs centripetal force
For orbits, gravitational attraction provides this force
Force points towards the centre (the larger body)
Object continuously "falls" around the central body
An orbiting object has velocity perpendicular to gravity
Gravity pulls it towards the centre
Result: curved path that never hits the surface
Fire a cannonball horizontally from a mountain
With enough speed, Earth curves away as fast as it falls
It continually falls but never lands—it's in orbit

content.text: Orbital period depends on orbital radius:
Further from centre = longer orbital period
Moon takes 27.3 days to orbit Earth
Neptune takes 165 years to orbit Sun
Formed with or captured by their planet
Explain why a satellite in a higher orbit has a longer orbital period.
Gravitational force is weaker at greater distance
Combination of slower speed and longer path gives longer period
, so larger radius means longer period.
Describe two differences between a geostationary satellite and a satellite in polar orbit.
Geostationary: orbits above equator, period = 24 hours
Polar: orbits over poles, period typically 90-120 minutes
Geostationary: appears stationary, always above same point
Polar: moves relative to Earth's surface, covers different areas
A satellite orbits Earth at 400 km altitude. If Earth's radius is 6400 km and orbital speed at this altitude is 7.7 km/s, calculate the orbital period.
Why must a geostationary satellite orbit above the equator?
For the satellite to appear stationary, it must stay above the same point on Earth
The satellite must orbit in the same plane as Earth's rotation
Earth rotates around its polar axis
The only orbit in this plane is above the equator
Any orbit not over the equator would oscillate north and south relative to the ground
is the minimum speed needed to escape a planet's gravitational field without further propulsion.
— Gravity acts on satellites. They're in free fall, continuously falling around Earth.
— They experience ~90% of surface gravity. They appear weightless because they're in free fall with the station.
— The satellite moves at ~3 km/s, but in sync with Earth's rotation.
"Satellites need fuel to stay in orbit"
— In the vacuum of space, no fuel is needed to maintain orbit (though some is needed to correct for small perturbations).
"All satellites are the same distance from Earth"
— Satellites orbit at many different altitudes depending on their purpose.

Astronauts on the ISS are NOT in zero gravity. Gravity at 400 km altitude is still about 90% of the surface value. They appear weightless because they are in free fall along with the station -- both falling at the same rate.
Orbital motion: gravitational force provides centripetal force
Closer orbits: faster speed, shorter period
Further orbits: slower speed, longer period
Low Earth Orbit (LEO): 200-2000 km, quick orbits
Polar orbit: passes over poles, covers whole Earth
Satellite uses: communication, navigation, weather, observation, research
Weightlessness in orbit: result of free fall, not absence of gravity
Escape velocity: speed needed to leave gravitational field
